hero.title: Winning in Style
hero.lede: Choose your cards. Build a deck. Play.

sections.heading: Pick 1 card, pass the pack to the left
body: Keep one card, then pass the rest. Your next choice comes from the pack your neighbor passes you.
You don't have to settle on colors right away. Good cards coming late can help you see what's available.

sections.heading: Answer their best card.
body: Take a few cheap answers, not just threats. Removal can stop their best creature or clear a blocker so you can attack.
Destroy, exile, bounce, and counterspells all help, but they don't do the same job. Bounce buys time; a counterspell must catch the spell before it resolves.

sections.heading: Build a 40-card deck.
body: Start with 17 lands + 23 nonlands.
Lands let you cast your spells; nonlands give you things to do. Staying at 40 cards helps you draw your best cards more often. Add basic lands after drafting.
Adjust for your curve and game plan, not one unlucky opening hand. There isn't one creature count that fits every deck.

sections.heading: Play before turn four.
body: Look for several plays at two and three mana. They let you join the game early instead of watching your opponent build a board.
A cheap creature or removal spell can help now and still leave mana for another spell later. A combat trick needs a creature and the right moment, so don't count it as your whole early game.

sections.heading: Find a strategy.
body: These are starting points, not commitments. You can combine ideas when your cards and mana support them.

sections.heading: Before game one.
body: Unused cards become your sideboard.

sections.heading: Fix first. Add colors later.
body: Fixing gives you permission to play more colors.
A great spell doesn't help much if it stays in your hand. Take the lands and fixing that let you cast the cards you want to play.

sections.heading: Count sources, not just basics.
body: Need a color early? About 9 sources is a starting point. Need it later? Around 6. One late splash card? Around 3.
These are rough guidelines, not guarantees. Multiple colored symbols and early spells need stronger support.
A dual land can supply either of its colors. A fetch only helps if your deck has a land it can find.
Mana creatures and Treasure makers are conditional: you must cast or create them first. If green casts your fixing, support green before adding other colors.

sections.heading: Have a way through.
body: Have a few ways to keep making progress when the ground fills up. Flying, menace, trample, unblockable attackers, or removal can help you get through.
They can be cards you already wanted to play. You don't need a separate pile of expensive finishers.

sections.heading: Draft a deck, not a pile.
body: Think about how your cards work together. Are you attacking early, building toward a big turn, or answering threats until you can take over?
You don't need a perfect combo. A deck with reliable mana and useful early plays can work well without much synergy.

sections.heading: Which colors can this card help with?
body: A Forest gives you green mana.
Breeding Pool can give you green or blue. It is still one land and makes one mana per tap, not both colors at once. It enters tapped unless you pay 2 life.
Windswept Heath finds a Forest or Plains in your library. Breeding Pool has the Forest type, so it can be a target too. No target left means no mana from the fetch.
Llanowar Elves is not a land. You need green mana to cast it before it can help, and it cannot tap immediately unless it has haste.

sections.heading: Lands and nonlands
body: Start with 17 lands + 23 nonlands.
Your curve and your fixing may call for a different balance. The deck stays at 40 cards in this illustration.

sections.heading: Stuck on a pick?
body: Need another color? Look for fixing. Missing early plays? Look for something cheaper. Can't handle their threats? Take an answer. Otherwise, choose a card that helps your plan.

sections.heading: Want some numbers to start with?
body: Start with 17 lands and 23 nonlands. Within those nonlands, an example to check against is five two-mana plays, four three-mana plays, four answers, and three ways through a stall.
These are example counts, not quotas or a proven best list. Roles overlap: a cheap removal spell can be an early play and an answer. A flying creature can be an early play and a way through.

Frank Karsten's Arena Cube midrange example uses about five two-drops and five three-drops. His aggressive example starts much lower. Borrow the idea of a busy early curve, not a fixed creature recipe.
Why several of each? You won't draw every card. One early creature or one answer won't reliably show up when you need it. Check your pile between packs and fill the gaps.

Mana is a separate check: roughly 9 sources for a main color, 6 for a later secondary color, or 3 for one late splash are starting guidelines, not guarantees. Early double-colored costs need more. See the mana explanation before adding another color.

sections.heading: Advice worth keeping
body: LSV, on Vintage Cube: "There is no shortage of powerful cards". His point: choose cards that work toward the deck you are building, rather than collecting impressive cards with no shared plan.
Caleb Durward: "When in doubt on a pick, hedging towards the cheaper card". Check what your deck is missing before your next pick: early plays, interaction, or fixing.

Reid Duke: "There's no 'master formula' for how many cards of each mana cost you should play." Your plan and the speed of the games matter. The example counts above are a place to begin, not a test you have to pass.

plans.name: Blink
plans.body: You get more out of creatures whose abilities trigger when they enter. Blink them to use those abilities again.

plans.name: Aristocrats
plans.body: Look for creatures you don't mind losing, and cards that reward you when they die.

plans.name: Counters + go wide
plans.body: Make several creatures, then improve them together with counters. A small board can turn into a real attack.

plans.name: Artifact sacrifice
plans.body: An artifact can do a job twice: once when it enters, and again when you sacrifice it for another effect.

plans.name: +1/+1 counters
plans.body: +1/+1 counters let your smaller creatures keep growing. Look for cards that add counters and cards that multiply them.

plans.name: Power 4+
plans.body: Creatures with at least four power turn on cards like The Earth King. Get that board in place, then attack.

plans.name: Delirium
plans.body: Delirium needs four card types in your graveyard. Cards that mill you can help turn it on.

plans.name: Humans
plans.body: Humans can make each other stronger. Cheap Humans let you build the board before cards like Thalia's Lieutenant reward you.

plans.name: Noncombat damage
plans.body: Small damage adds up. Pair repeatable damage from cards like Firebrand Archer with effects that make each hit larger.

plans.name: Theft
plans.body: You can use an opponent's spells as part of your own plan. Keep enough interaction to reach the turn when it matters.

plans.name: Five-color good stuff
plans.body: Draft fixing early. Build a strong base color. Splash powerful cards when your mana supports them; five colors is an option, not a requirement.
